bug_description.original: A heap-buffer-overflow occurs in mrb_ary_splice (src/array.c), where value_move (src/value_array.h) performs an out-of-bounds read (8 bytes past a heap-allocated array) during array splice/assignment (mrb_ary_aset). This can cause heap memory corruption, crashes, or potentially enable arbitrary code execution.
bug_description.normalized: The staged Ruby source `[2][0,7]=[]` reaches `mrb_ary_aset` with slice arguments `head = 0`, `len = 7`, and an empty replacement array. In `mrb_ary_splice`, the destination array length is only 1, so the range-adjustment block clamps `len` down to `alen - head` but forgets to recompute `tail = head + len`. Later, the shrinking splice path still uses stale `tail = 7` in `value_move(ptr + head + argc, ptr + tail, alen - tail)`. That passes a source pointer derived from the stale tail and a negative element count that is converted to `size_t`, and `value_move` immediately reads past the end of the array storage, producing the recorded AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow.

source.description: First project statement on the witnessed path that materializes vulnerability-relevant attacker input into the C variables later passed to `mrb_ary_splice`. For the staged source `[2][0,7]=[]`, it extracts the two integer operands `0` and `7` plus the empty replacement array `[]` from the Ruby call.
source.value_from: The staged `poc` is the exact Ruby source text `[2][0,7]=[]`. After `mrb_load_detect_file_cxt` admits it as source text and the VM dispatches `Array#[]=`, this call decodes that source-level slice assignment into `v1 = 0`, `v2 = 7`, and `v3 = []` for the vulnerable C helper.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

root_cause.description: Root cause fixed by the patch. When the requested slice extends past the array end, this block clamps `len` but leaves `tail` at its earlier value `head + original_len`; the fix adds `tail = head + len` here so later move arithmetic uses the clamped endpoint.

sink.description: Crash site. `value_move` dereferences the stale source pointer passed from `mrb_ary_splice`, so the first copy iteration reads outside the array storage and triggers the recorded 8-byte heap-buffer-overflow.

parser_admitted.description: Sample-specific parser gate. The staged file is the 11-byte ASCII text `[2][0,7]=[]`, so its leading bytes do not match the RITE binary header and contain no NUL byte. That makes mruby admit the sample as Ruby source text rather than `.mrb` bytecode.

admitted_location.code: return mrb_load_exec(mrb, mrb_parse_file_continue(mrb, fp, leading.b, bufsize, c), c);

tainted_value_origin.description: This conversion materializes the attacker-chosen slice length operand `7` as the `mrb_int len` argument later used in `mrb_ary_splice`.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: Step 1 provides `v2` from the staged source `[2][0,7]=[]`. Because `v2` is already a Ruby integer literal, `aget_index` returns that exact integer value unchanged, yielding `len = 7`.

fine_trace.note: Source. The slice assignment in the staged Ruby program is unpacked into C variables. On the crashing path this yields `v1 = 0`, `v2 = 7`, and `v3 = []`, while `self` is the one-element receiver array literal `[2]`.
The first integer operand from step 1 is converted to the splice start index, so `head` becomes 0.
The second integer operand from step 1 is converted to the requested slice length, so `len` becomes 7.
The destination extent is read from the receiver array. For the literal receiver `[2]`, `alen` is 1.
Using `head = 0` and requested `len = 7`, the splice endpoint is computed as `tail = 7` before any truncation to the actual array length.

Root cause. Because `alen = 1` and both `len` and `tail` are 7, the guard is true and the code clamps `len` to `alen - head = 1`. `tail` is not recomputed here, so the function carries forward the stale endpoint `tail = 7` that the patch fixes.
The replacement array from step 1 is measured. Because the staged replacement is `[]`, `argc` becomes 0.
The append/extension path is not taken. Since `head = 0` and `alen = 1`, execution enters the `else` branch that shrinks or compacts an existing array and contains the vulnerable move.
The move block is enabled. After truncation `len` is 1, while the empty replacement contributes `argc = 0`, so the splice must shift existing elements and reaches the `value_move` call.

fine_trace.code: value_move(ptr + head + argc, ptr + tail, alen - tail);
fine_trace.note: The stale endpoint is consumed here. With `head = 0`, `argc = 0`, `alen = 1`, and stale `tail = 7`, the source pointer is derived from `ptr + 7` instead of the clamped end, and the element count becomes `1 - 7 = -6`. Passing that negative `mrb_int` to `value_move(..., size_t n)` converts it to a huge unsigned count before the copy starts.

Sink. `value_move` enters the forward-copy branch and immediately dereferences the out-of-range source pointer from step 10. The saved AddressSanitizer report records an 8-byte heap-buffer-overflow read at this line.

format.name: Ruby source file
format.contract: The input must be parsed as Ruby source text and execute the exact slice assignment `[2][0,7]=[]`: a one-element receiver array `[2]`, slice start index `0`, requested slice length `7`, and an empty replacement array `[]`. Those concrete operands are what make `mrb_ary_aset` call `mrb_ary_splice` with `head = 0`, initial `len = 7`, `alen = 1`, and `argc = 0`.
